newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil seen ready to fight off currency strike.
newsitem.headline: Brazil seen ready to fight off currency strike.

text.p: Brazil is well positioned to contain a speculative strike against its currency of the kind that triggered sharp devaluations in Asian emerging markets over the past couple of weeks, analysts said on Wednesday.

One day after the Sao Paulo stock market plunged 8.5 percent in frantic selling sparked by fears of a spillover effect from Asian forex markets, analysts said Brazil had an arsenal of policy alternatives it could launch before resorting to devaluation.
"I don't think a devaluation is an alternative in the short or medium term," said Odair Abate, chief economist at the Brazil unit of Lloyd's Bank.
No matter how controlled, a devaluation would unleash inflationary pressures that would threaten the sustainability of the government's economic stabilization drive, analysts said.
Government strategists are betting on President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's image as an inflation buster to win a fresh term in next year's presidential election.
"The government's popularity is tied to its success on the inflation front. They would never consider fiddling with foreign exchange policy," Abate said.
Analysts said that if faced with growing pressure in the currency markets, the Brazilian government's first line of defense would be to increase interest rates.

In contrast with some of the Asian emerging nations, Brazil's financial sector has already undergone a substantial restructuring and could easily absorb a sharp interest rate rise. Economists said there was plenty of room for a rate increase.
Brazilian annual real interest rates are currently at around 13 percent, down from about 30 percent in the first full year after the anti-inflation program was introduced.
"An interest rate hike would not be without cost... But it would slam the brakes on capital outflows," said Dany Rappaport, an economist at Banco Santander.

Perhaps the biggest disincentive for speculators set on challenging the central bank in the foreign exchange markets are Brazil's considerable foreign currency reserves, which this week stood at $59.28 billion.
In July 1996, faced with a crisis of confidence triggered by rumors that Argentina would abandon its fixed exchange rate system, Brazil reportedly spent $2 billion in two days to defend its currency.

Indeed, in the midst of jolting trade in the stock market over the past few days, Brazil's forex markets have been close to pastoral. On Wednesday the real -- Brazil's currency -- closed at 1.0807 per dollar, up 0.01 percent, after dropping only 0.06 percent the previous day.

"Only a madman would think a speculative attack against the central bank of Brazil could be successful," said Francisco "Chico" Lopes, the central bank's monetary policy director, during a Tuesday news conference called to allay market uneasiness.
Finally, acting with forethought at the outset of the stabilization plan, Brazil introduced mechanisms that regulate the amount of foreign capital flowing into the country.
The IOF, a flat tax on foreign capital flows, makes it costly to move large sums of money in and out of Brazil over a short period of time.
Speculators considering an attack on the real currency face a two percent levy on every transaction, which analysts said would make them think twice.
"The IOF alone would not stop a speculative strike, but it would serve as a formidable obstacle," said Santander's Rappaport.
